strengths: Well-motivated problem: the paper identifies and quantifies a real issue (up to 30% preference conflicts in UltraFeedback) with aggregating fine-grained preference signals, and clearly articulates why single holistic 'better-than' judgments are insufficient.

Solid theoretical contribution: DMPO is derived cleanly from the multi-preference PPO objective, and the paper provides rigorous proofs (via several supporting lemmas and an exchange argument) establishing loss bounds and the optimality of selecting samples with the most negative PD term, going beyond a purely heuristic data selection rule.

Practical operationalization is thoughtful: the cross-pseudo reward estimation scheme (using smaller proxy models with quantile normalization) and explicit length-bias mitigation (balanced sampling + reward penalty) directly address realistic obstacles in computing the theoretical PD term.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three conflict levels, multiple baselines (Overall, Oracle, ALL, DMPO, RAND, HIGH, MID), two evaluation protocols (AlpacaEval2 and pairwise LLM-judged win rate across five diverse test sets), and selection-budget sensitivity analysis.
Notably, the method outperforms the annotation-intensive Oracle baseline while using only 30% of the data and less compute, which is a strong and practically significant result if it holds up.

Ablations (A1: ignoring fine-grained structure, A2: no length-bias correction) and appendix analyses (reward prediction conflict heatmaps, selected-sample length distributions) provide good support for the specific design choices (fine-grained modeling and de-biasing) rather than just showing an aggregate improvement.
Extensive appendix with full derivations, proofs, and additional experiments improves reproducibility and rigor.
weaknesses: All experiments use a single dataset (UltraFeedback) and largely one alignment model/proxy model pair (Llama-3.1-8B / Llama-3.2-3B), so generalization across other preference datasets, domains, or model families is untested.

The 'conflict level' datasets are synthetically constructed by randomly assigning a single sub-preference criterion to each pair rather than sourced from genuinely independent annotation processes per aspect; this simulated setup may not fully capture real-world noise/conflict patterns in naturally collected fine-grained preference data.

The surprising result that the method beats the Oracle (average of ground-truth fine-grained scores) deserves more explanation/analysis—it's unclear whether this stems from genuine noise-filtering benefits or from confounds such as length-bias interactions with the LLM judges (Qwen2-Max, GPT-4o) used for evaluation.

The 'mild condition' required for Theorem 3.7 (2(κ−1)/κ · r ≤ c2−c0) is asserted but not empirically verified to hold for the actual trained models/rewards, leaving a gap between the theoretical guarantee and its applicability in the reported experiments.

The selection budget (30%) is used as the primary operating point without a principled method for choosing it per dataset; Figure 3 shows performance is budget-sensitive and can plateau/decline, suggesting practical tuning is needed that is not addressed as a limitation in the main text.

The 'all-in-one' proxy reward model (single backbone with different system prompts per sub-preference) is a nontrivial design choice that could introduce interference across sub-preference reward estimates, but this choice is not separately ablated against fully independent reward models.

Reliance on a single LLM judge (Qwen2-Max) for the pairwise evaluation and a single automated benchmark (AlpacaEval2) leaves open concerns about evaluator bias (e.g., length or style preferences) affecting the reported win-rate improvements, despite order-swapping mitigation.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated and underexplored problem: how to leverage aggregated fine-grained (aspect-specific) preference data for DPO-style alignment when such data contains inter-aspect conflicts.

It provides a full theoretical derivation from a multi-preference PPO objective to the DMPO loss and the Preference Divergence (PD) term, and proves loss bounds (Theorems 3.6/3.7) that formally justify selecting high-consensus (most-negative-PD) samples rather than optimizing PD directly.

The proposed PD estimation pipeline (cross-pseudo reward extrapolation with a smaller proxy model) and the length-bias mitigation techniques (balanced sampling + length-penalized reward loss) are practical engineering solutions that connect the theory to an implementable algorithm.

The empirical study is reasonably thorough: multiple conflict levels, two evaluation protocols (AlpacaEval2 and pairwise LLM-judge across 5 test sets), selection-budget sweeps, ablations on fine-grained modeling and length-bias correction, and extensive appendix analyses (reward conflict heatmaps, PD/reward-gap distributions, selected-sample length distributions).
Efficiency gains are demonstrated: the method uses only 30% of the data yet outperforms full-dataset training and an annotation-heavy oracle, which is a practically appealing result if it holds up.
weaknesses: All experiments are derived from a single base dataset (UltraFeedback); the three 'conflict levels' are synthetically constructed by the authors themselves (re-pairing responses and randomly assigning a sub-preference label), rather than using genuinely independent fine-grained preference datasets, which raises concerns about how representative these controlled splits are of real-world aggregated preference data and limits generalizability of the conclusions.

There is a risk of circularity/leakage: the same UltraFeedback aspect annotations are used both to construct the synthetic 'conflicting' labels and to train the proxy reward models used for PD estimation, so the strong results may partly reflect this closed loop rather than a method that would generalize to genuinely noisy, independently collected fine-grained preference data.

The comparison baselines for the 'selection' setting (RAND, HIGH, MID) are all ad hoc variants the authors themselves define around their own PD term, rather than actual published data-selection methods for DPO/RLHF cited in the related work section (e.g., Deng et al. 2025, Lee et al. 2025, Gao et al. 2025), so the paper does not empirically demonstrate superiority over existing selection approaches in the literature.

Evaluation relies entirely on a single LLM judge (Qwen2-Max, and GPT-4o for AlpacaEval2) with no human evaluation or agreement study, leaving open the possibility that judge biases (e.g., toward certain styles despite length-control attempts) affect the reported gains, especially given the paper's own admission that pairwise evaluation is less robust to length bias.

The theoretical guarantees rest on multiple strong/idealized assumptions (per-aspect latent reward models with clean BT structure, known ϕk, bounded and well-behaved preference margins, normalized rewards, a 'mild condition' 2(κ-1)r/κ ≤ c2-c0) that are unverifiable in practice; the gap between this idealized theory and the heuristic practical estimator (quantile scaling, clipping to [-1,1], all-in-one proxy reward model with prompt-based specialization) is not rigorously bridged or empirically validated (e.g., no correlation analysis between estimated and 'true' PD values).

Only a single base model (Llama-3.1-8B) and a single proxy model (Llama-3.2-3B) are evaluated; there is no evidence the method generalizes across model families/sizes or to other alignment algorithms beyond vanilla DPO.

The default selection budget of 30% used in the main table appears arbitrarily chosen without principled justification, even though Theorem 3.7 does not specify an optimal budget; the budget-sweep results also show diminishing/mixed advantages over ablations at larger budgets (Appendix Table B.1-B.3), weakening the strength of the main claims.

The paper's framing occasionally overstates conclusions (e.g., claiming to 'unlock the potential of robust LLM alignment' and obviate holistic annotation) based on a single synthetic-dataset study, which is a fairly narrow empirical basis for such broad claims.

strengths: Novel data-centric framing of multi-preference alignment: rather than directly optimizing a weighted multi-preference objective (DMPO), the paper uses the derived Preference Divergence (PD) term as a principled criterion for data selection, which is a clean and practically useful insight.

Solid theoretical development: the paper derives the DMPO objective from a multi-preference PPO objective, formalizes the data selection problem, and proves loss bounds (Theorem 3.6) and an optimal selection strategy (Theorem 3.7) via careful convexity/monotonicity/exchange arguments in the appendix.

Comprehensive empirical validation across three synthetic conflict levels (10/20/30%) with multiple relevant baselines (Overall, Oracle, ALL, DMPO, RAND, HIGH, MID), showing the proposed PD selection method outperforms even the annotation-heavy Oracle baseline while using less compute.

Practical methodology contributions (cross-pseudo reward estimation with a smaller proxy model, length-balanced sampling, and explicit length-penalty in reward loss) that address real implementation obstacles and are validated via targeted ablations (A1, A2) showing length-bias mitigation matters.

Thorough supplementary analysis in the appendix (PD/reward-gap distributions, selection budget sweeps, selected-sample length distributions, per-dataset win scores) that strengthens confidence in the reported trends and mechanism explanations.
weaknesses: The three conflict-level datasets are synthetically constructed by controlling sub-preference sampling weights from a single source (UltraFeedback), rather than using naturally occurring multi-source fine-grained preference data; this raises questions about how well the findings generalize to real, more heterogeneous fine-grained preference collections.

All main alignment experiments use a single base model (Llama-3.1-8B) and a single proxy reward model (Llama-3.2-3B); no results are shown across different model scales/families, limiting confidence in the generality of the improvements.

The theoretical guarantees rely on several nontrivial assumptions (bounded preference margins in specific ranges, a mild condition relating r, κ, c0, c2, known ϕk) whose validity in the actual experimental setting is not empirically verified, making the practical tightness/relevance of the bounds unclear.

The practical PD estimation departs substantially from the idealized setting used in the theory (approximate cross-pseudo rewards, quantile normalization, clipping), yet the paper offers no direct quantitative check of estimation error/quality against ground-truth PD values beyond the length-bias ablations.

Automatic evaluation relies entirely on LLM-as-judge (Qwen2-Max, GPT-4o) and AlpacaEval2 without human evaluation, and the paper itself notes pairwise evaluation is susceptible to length bias, leaving open whether reported gains partly reflect judge-model idiosyncrasies rather than genuine quality improvements.

Selection budget (30%) is fixed as the headline configuration; while a budget sweep is provided, there is no principled/automatic way proposed to choose the budget in practice without access to held-out evaluation, which limits real-world applicability.

Comparisons for the selection step are limited to simple heuristics (RAND/HIGH/MID) constructed by the authors rather than adapting existing state-of-the-art DPO/RLHF data-selection baselines (e.g., LESS-style influence-based or difficulty-based selection cited in related work) to the multi-preference setting, which would better contextualize the improvement.
